name: Hassan Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hassan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, okay. I'm not sure I'll have clever answers, but I'll be straight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Karim, a family friend from our mosque, who has a small firm doing house extensions and loft conversions. There's four of us, and I do the carpentry, the roof joists, the floors, the stud walls, and I help with the blocks when we're short. I start at half seven and Karim picks me up in the van. I like finishing an extension and seeing a family move their table into it, but the winter mornings are hard on the hands.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home and with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm getting married next summer, to Samira. I still live with my parents to save, but the wedding has taken most of it, so right now I've got maybe a month's money if that. The pay with Karim isn't high, but he's fair and he's family, more or less. There aren't many building firms in our part of town, and I've never used any of these AI things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So nothing much changes. Good. I like things as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I always thought it was too good to be true. A computer can't put up a roof. I'd tell the lads to get on with the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI isn't what keeps me up. My fiancée Samira and I have paid the deposit on the wedding hall, and that was most of my savings gone in one afternoon. And Karim has fewer extension jobs booked for spring than last year, because people can't afford to borrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work every hour Karim gives me and take weekend jobs from people at the mosque, fixing doors and fences. I'd cut out buying lunch and eat what my mum packs. And I'd ask my uncle if he needs a hand on his rental flats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but about money and the wedding, not about computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if spring is quiet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then Karim keeps the older men on first, which is right, they have families. I'd be the one doing odd jobs. We'd maybe make the wedding smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for work further away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the city, but that means leaving Karim, and he gave me my start. My dad would say loyalty counts. I'd only go if I really had to.

A computer can't **put up a roof**, so workmates should get on with the work.

Ask his **uncle** for work on his rental flats.
feel: **Worried** about money and the wedding, not about computers.

Fix doors and fences for mosque families at weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office people get it first. We don't have office people, it's Karim and his notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for big companies, not small firms like ours. Customers want to shake the hand of the man building their extension. I'd say people should work hard and they'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a computer can price an extension, but it can't knock on a neighbour's door and calm them down about the noise. But I don't know. Maybe the big firms get cheaper with all their software and win the jobs we would have got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do. If Karim wanted to try an app for quotes, I'd let him, but I wouldn't touch it myself. I'd save more for after the wedding and maybe skip the honeymoon abroad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like the ground is moving under someone else's house and you wonder if yours is next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the big firms might get cheaper. What would that mean for Karim?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer jobs, lower prices, longer hours. Karim is 55 and he might just stop. Then I'm looking for work with no firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn to use an AI tool if Karim asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If he really needed it, yes, for him. But I'd be slow. My younger brother Tariq is good with that stuff, I'd probably ask him to show me.

Customers want to **shake hands** with the builder, and hard work still pays.

fieldNote: Hands-on work looks safe, but **price competition** could close Karim's firm: **anxious**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 a robot can do what I do? I find that hard to believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll believe it when I see it. People said the same about many things. I'd tell the lads to trust in God and keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, if it's true, it frightens me. If robots are laying blocks by 2031, I don't know what kind of husband I'd be to my fiancée Samira with no trade. The thinking part of Karim's job goes in 2028, but my part goes three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Samira and both our families about pushing the wedding back a year, so we don't start married life in debt. I'd keep working for Karim as long as he has work. I'd ask the elders at the mosque what other men are doing, because they know everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and ashamed of being frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ashamed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a man should be able to provide. My dad never said he was scared. I'd feel like I was failing before I started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Samira say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say we'll manage, she works too, at a pharmacy. But a pharmacy is lots of checking and answering customers, so maybe her job changes in 2028 as well. That makes it worse, not better.

People said the **same** about many things before.
Workmates should **trust in God** and keep working.
think: Robots laying blocks by **2031** would leave him with **no trade**.
The thinking side goes in 2028, his **hands-on part** three years later.
do: Ask both families about pushing the **wedding back** a year.
Keep working for **Karim** as long as there's work.
Ask **mosque elders** what other men are doing.
S2.quote: If robots are laying blocks by 2031, I don't know what kind of husband I'd be to my fiancée Samira with no trade.
fieldNote: Public **disbelief** covers private fear about providing as a husband.
Realises Samira's **pharmacy** job is exposed too: **alarmed**.
Turns to **family and faith community**, not government.

steps.text: Ask both families about moving the wedding back a year
Keep working for Karim while extension jobs last
Ask the mosque elders about work for men in his trade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2034. I'd be 35, married, maybe a child by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, and men should learn a second skill like their fathers did. I'd say the government should get out of the way and let firms train apprentices. No handouts, proper work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my dad worked in the same factory for thirty years, and I thought building would give me the same kind of life. Now I don't know what kind of life it gives me. Five years feels like a long time until I think about the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with Karim and save harder after the wedding. I'd maybe do a plumbing course at night, because pipes in old houses are fiddly and people still want a man they trust. I'd put off having children until things are clearer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Worried for the family I don't have yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said plumbing. Would robots not reach that too by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe they would. I don't know enough to say. I'm just thinking of something my hands can do in a stranger's house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'll be fine, because they worry. My mum would pray for me. My dad would tell me to work harder, and I would.

feel: **Heavy**, worried for a family he doesn't have yet.

fieldNote: Expects his trade gone by 2034 with no savings and few firms: **alarmed**.
Admits he doesn't know if **plumbing** is safer.
Traditional views on **providing** and **apprenticeships** shape his answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's 2036, robots 2039. I'll be close to 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, there's no point worrying. Get married, work hard, raise a family. That's what I'd tell anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is a long time. I'd rather spend it working hard than worrying about machines I've never seen. But I know I'd do nothing until it's close, and that worries me a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married next summer as planned. I'd keep working for Karim and maybe take over some of the firm when he retires, if he trusts me. I'd save a bit each month for a family home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, mostly. Still nervous about money, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Taking over from Karim. Would you have to deal with the office side then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the quotes, the ordering, the paperwork. I'd probably need Tariq or Samira to help with the computer side. Karim does it on paper now and I'd want to keep it simple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about money in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, tight. Ten years without robots doesn't make Karim's prices higher. We'd live simply and save.

People should get married, **work hard** and raise a family.

fieldNote: The distant date calms him about robots, but **tight money** keeps him **anxious**.

steps.text: Marry Samira next summer as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be newly married with no trade and maybe Samira's job changing too. What would help is firms being allowed and paid to take on apprentices in whatever comes next, so men can learn on the job instead of sitting in a classroom or on benefits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about pride. I don't want a handout. I want a job where I'm tired at the end of the day and my family is proud of me.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout. I want a job where I'm tired at the end of the day and my family is proud of me.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old carpenter** building extensions for a family friend's small firm.
He's **engaged** to Samira, and the wedding deposit took most of his savings.
He never uses **AI** and leans on family and mosque networks for work and advice.
He favours **hard work and apprenticeships** over handouts, and fears failing as a provider.
Already **anxious**, he becomes **alarmed** when robots arrive by 2031 or 2034.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be newly married with no trade.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **apprenticeships** in new trades, learned on the job rather than in a classroom.
